questions.q: Authentication vs authorisation vs accounting: define each precisely, explain principals, credentials and claims, and show why conflating authN and authZ causes breaches.
questions.a:
### Definitions
- **Authentication (authN)**: proving who (or what) is calling: user, service, device. Output: an authenticated **principal** with claims.
- **Authorisation (authZ)**: deciding whether that principal may perform this action on this resource now.
- **Accounting / audit**: recording who did what, when, with which outcome.

### Vocabulary
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Identity | a set of attributes about a subject (customer, employee, workload) |
| Credential | proof used to authenticate (password, passkey, certificate, federated assertion) |
| Principal | the authenticated subject in a request ({{ClaimsPrincipal}}) |
| Claim | an assertion about the subject (sub, email, roles, tenant, amr) issued by a trusted party |
| Entitlement | a permission granted (role, scope, relationship) |

### Why conflation hurts
"Logged in" is not "allowed". Most API breaches (BOLA) happen because code checks authentication only. Equally, putting authorisation data into authentication tokens (huge role lists, account ids) creates stale, oversized tokens and decisions that ignore current state (revoked access lingers until expiry).

### Rule
Authenticate once at the edge and in every service; authorise at every decision point using current context.
pts: AuthN proves identity; authZ decides access; audit records it.
Principals carry claims from trusted issuers.
Logged in is not allowed: BOLA comes from authN-only checks.
Don't overload tokens with authorisation data.
Authorise at every decision point with current context.
questions.ex: An internal tool granted any authenticated employee access to customer accounts because the developer assumed SSO meant authorisation. An audit found 3,000 employees could view balances; entitlement checks per action restricted it to 120 support staff.

What claims belong in an access token?
How do you audit authorisation?

questions.q: Compare RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC and policy-based access control. Which fits a retail bank's staff app, a corporate banking portal and a document-sharing feature?
questions.a:
| Model | Decision based on | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RBAC** | roles assigned to users ({{teller}}, {{branch-manager}}) | simple, auditable | role explosion when context matters (branch, region, amount) |
| **ABAC** | attributes of subject, resource, action, environment ({{user.branch == account.branch && amount < user.limit}}) | expressive, contextual | harder to audit "who can access X"; attribute quality matters |
| **ReBAC** | relationships ({{user is approver of company}}, {{company owns account}}) | natural for sharing, hierarchies, delegation | needs a relationship store and graph evaluation |
| **PBAC** | policies as code evaluated by an engine (OPA Rego, Cedar), using any of the above | central, testable, versioned policies | another system to run and integrate |

### Fits
- **Retail staff app**: RBAC for coarse permissions plus ABAC conditions (same branch, limits by grade, working hours).
- **Corporate banking portal**: ReBAC (users belong to companies, companies own accounts, mandates define who can approve what) plus ABAC for amount thresholds.
- **Document sharing**: ReBAC (owner, shared-with, inherited folder permissions).

### Reality
Most systems combine: roles as one attribute, relationships for ownership, attributes for context, policies to express it all consistently.
pts: RBAC: simple, but explodes with context.
ABAC: attributes and context; audit is harder.
ReBAC: relationships for ownership, sharing, delegation.
PBAC: policies as code in an engine.
Real systems combine models.
questions.ex: A bank created a role per branch per grade per product ("teller-london-g3-mortgages") and reached 14,000 roles. Moving to 40 roles plus branch and grade attributes in policies cut roles by 99% and made access reviews possible.

questions.q: Explain ASP.NET Core's authorisation model (policies, requirements, handlers, fallback and default policies) and how to structure it for a large API.
questions.a:
### Building blocks
- **Requirement**: a marker describing what must be true ({{MinimumApprovalLimitRequirement}}).
- **Handler**: logic that evaluates requirements against the user (and optionally a resource); calls {{context.Succeed}}; multiple handlers can satisfy one requirement (OR), multiple requirements in a policy must all pass (AND).
- **Policy**: named set of requirements, schemes and claims checks.
- **Default policy**: used by {{[Authorize]}} without a name.
- **Fallback policy**: applied to endpoints with **no** authorisation metadata: set it to require authenticated users so new endpoints are secure by default.
- **Resource-based authorisation**: {{IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, requirement)}} inside handlers when the decision needs the loaded resource.

### Structuring for a large API
- Policies named by **capability** ({{payments.approve}}), not by role, so role changes don't touch code.
- Map capabilities to roles or scopes in one place (configuration or a policy provider).
- Resource-based handlers for object-level checks.
- A custom {{IAuthorizationPolicyProvider}} for parameterised policies (thresholds).
- Tests per policy and per handler.
pts: Requirements, handlers, policies.
Handlers OR within a requirement; requirements AND within a policy.
Fallback policy makes new endpoints secure.
Name policies by capability.
Resource-based handlers for object checks.
questions.ex: A new endpoint shipped without [Authorize] and exposed payment details to anonymous callers. Setting a fallback policy requiring authenticated users made every future endpoint secure by default; AllowAnonymous usages became reviewable exceptions.
fu: How do custom policy providers work?
How do you test handlers?
How do multiple handlers interact?
pit: Object checks in controllers ad hoc.

questions.q: Where should a user's roles and permissions come from at runtime: token claims, groups, or a lookup? Explain claims transformation and the Entra ID groups overage problem.
questions.a:
### Options
| Source | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **App roles in the token** (assigned in the IdP) | simple, no lookup | stale until token refresh; limited context |
| **Group claims** | reuse directory groups | **overage**: Entra ID omits groups if the user has more than about 200 (JWT) and adds an overage indicator; group ids are opaque; leaks org structure |
| **Lookup at runtime** (entitlement service or database) | current, rich, contextual (branch, limits) | latency, caching, availability |
| **Hybrid** | coarse roles in token, fine-grained permissions looked up and cached | two places to manage |

### Claims transformation
{{IClaimsTransformation}} runs after authentication and can enrich the principal (load permissions from an entitlement service, map groups to app permissions). Cache results per user for minutes; beware it runs on every request (and possibly multiple times).

### Recommendations
Use **app roles** (not raw groups) for coarse application roles; keep tokens small; look up fine-grained and resource-specific entitlements at decision time; handle overage by calling Microsoft Graph only if you must use groups.
pts: App roles in tokens for coarse roles.
Groups claims suffer overage and opacity.
Look up fine-grained entitlements at runtime, cached.
IClaimsTransformation enriches principals.
Keep tokens small and decisions current.
questions.ex: A bank's admin portal relied on group claims; senior managers in 300 groups got tokens without groups (overage) and lost access on a Monday morning. Switching to app roles plus a cached entitlement lookup fixed it and shrank tokens from 9 KB to 1.5 KB.
fu: How long should entitlement caches live?
How do you invalidate on role change?
App roles vs groups in Entra ID?
pit: Relying on group claims at scale.

questions.q: SAML vs OpenID Connect vs WS-Federation: how do they work, when do you still meet each, and what should new applications use?
questions.a:
### SAML 2.0
XML-based assertions signed by the IdP, delivered via browser redirects or POSTs to the service provider. Strong in enterprise SSO and B2B federation; complex XML signature handling (signature wrapping attacks historically); no native API or mobile story.

### OpenID Connect
Identity layer on OAuth 2.0: JSON, JWT ID tokens, discovery documents, JWKS; works for web, SPA (with BFF), mobile and APIs (OAuth access tokens). Modern default.

### WS-Federation
Older Microsoft protocol (ADFS, SharePoint); legacy only.

### When you meet each
| Situation | Protocol |
|---|---|
| New web, mobile, API | **OIDC + OAuth 2.0** |
| Enterprise SaaS integrating with customers' IdPs | SAML still common; support both |
| Legacy on-prem apps behind ADFS | WS-Fed or SAML; migrate to Entra ID with OIDC |
| B2B partner portals | SAML or OIDC federation per partner |

### Key concepts regardless
Trust established by metadata (certificates or JWKS), audience restriction, short validity, clock skew, signature validation with maintained libraries, and **IdP-initiated** flows treated cautiously (CSRF and replay concerns).
questions.dia:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Browser
  participant A as App (relying party)
  participant I as Identity provider
  U->>A: GET /portal
  A-->>U: redirect to IdP authorize with state and nonce
  U->>I: authenticate (MFA)
  I-->>U: redirect back with code
  U->>A: callback with code
  A->>I: exchange code for ID token and access token
  I-->>A: tokens signed by IdP
  A->>A: validate signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry
  A-->>U: session cookie
pts: SAML: XML assertions, enterprise and B2B.
OIDC: JSON and JWT on OAuth 2.0, the modern default.
WS-Fed is legacy.
Trust via metadata, audience, short validity.
Use brokers instead of hand-rolled SAML.
questions.ex: A team hand-rolled SAML response validation and missed a signature wrapping case; a tester logged in as any user by injecting an unsigned assertion. Replacing it with a maintained identity broker closed the hole and added OIDC for the mobile app.

questions.q: Workforce identity, B2B identity and customer identity (CIAM) have different requirements. Compare them and the typical platforms for each.
questions.a:
| Aspect | Workforce | B2B (partners, corporate clients) | CIAM (retail customers) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Users | employees, contractors | users at other organisations | millions of consumers |
| Source of identity | HR system to directory | partner's own IdP (federation) or invitations | self-registration plus KYC |
| Authentication | SSO, phishing-resistant MFA, device compliance | federation or local accounts with MFA | passwords or passkeys, social login (rarely in banking), device binding |
| Lifecycle | joiner-mover-leaver from HR | partner admins manage their users; access reviews | self-service, account recovery, dormant accounts |
| Authorisation | roles, PIM, entitlements | delegated admin, per-organisation entitlements | per-customer data ownership, consents |
| Scale and UX | thousands, internal UX | thousands to tens of thousands | millions; conversion matters |
| Platforms | Entra ID, Okta Workforce | Entra ID B2B, Okta, broker per partner | Entra External ID, Auth0/Okta CIC, ForgeRock/Ping, custom on Duende IdentityServer |

### Design implications
Separate tenants or instances for workforce and customers (blast radius, different policies), consistent token formats for APIs, and a clear mapping from each identity type to authorisation models.
pts: Workforce, B2B and CIAM differ in source, lifecycle, scale.
Workforce: HR-driven, phishing-resistant MFA.
B2B: federation and delegated admin.
CIAM: self-service, KYC binding, conversion.
Separate tenants; distinct schemes and policies.
questions.ex: A bank put corporate client users into its workforce tenant as guests; conditional access policies meant for employees blocked them, and their accounts appeared in employee access reviews. A dedicated B2B identity setup with delegated admin removed both problems.
fu: Should staff and customers ever share a tenant?
How do partners manage their own users?
What CIAM features matter most for banks?
pit: One policy set for all identity types.
Mixing token issuers without scheme separation.

questions.q: Implement resource-based authorisation for accounts that can be owned, jointly held, or delegated (power of attorney). How do you keep it fast and correct?
questions.a:
### Model
An account has **parties** with relationships: owner, joint owner, delegate (with scope: view, pay up to a limit, until a date), plus staff access with a reason. Authorisation asks: does the caller have a relationship granting this operation, now?

### Implementation
- Load the resource with its relevant relationships (or query a relationship store) in one query.
- A handler per operation family evaluates relationships and constraints (limits, expiry).
- Return 404 for no access (don't reveal existence).
- Cache relationship lookups briefly or use relationship-aware queries ({{WHERE EXISTS party with customerId}}) for lists.

### Lists vs single objects
Filtering lists by authorisation must happen **in the query** (only accounts where the caller is a party), not by loading everything and filtering in memory.

### Correctness
- Expiry and revocation evaluated at decision time.
- Joint accounts: some operations need both owners (mandate rules).
- Tests for each relationship type and edge cases (expired delegation, revoked joint owner).
pts: Model relationships: owner, joint, delegate, staff.
Evaluate constraints like limits and expiry at decision time.
404 for no access.
Filter lists in the query.
Test every relationship type and edge case.
questions.ex: An expired power of attorney still allowed a delegate to view accounts because expiry was checked only at login. Evaluating ValidUntil in the handler and the list query closed it; tests now cover expired and revoked delegations.

questions.q: Centralised authorisation service (OPA, Cedar/Amazon Verified Permissions, OpenFGA) or in-process policies? Compare architectures and failure modes.
questions.a:
### Options
| Architecture | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **In-process policies** (ASP.NET Core handlers) | code in each service | fastest, no dependency | duplicated logic across services; hard to audit globally |
| **Policy library / sidecar** (OPA sidecar, Cedar embedded) | policies distributed as bundles, evaluated locally | central authoring, local evaluation (sub-ms) | bundle distribution, data sync for decisions |
| **Central decision service** (PDP over network) | services call it per decision | single place, consistent, easy audit | latency, availability dependency, scaling |
| **Relationship store** (OpenFGA, SpiceDB, Zanzibar-style) | services write relationships, ask "check" or "list objects" | ReBAC at scale, consistent model | data duplication, consistency tokens, operational complexity |

### Failure modes
- PDP unavailable: fail closed for writes and sensitive reads; cache recent allow decisions briefly only where risk allows.
- Stale data: relationships not yet propagated (use consistency tokens, Zookies in Zanzibar terms).
- Policy bugs affecting everyone at once: test suites and staged rollout of policy bundles.

### Recommendation
Central **authoring** (policies as code, tests, versions), **local evaluation** where possible (OPA or Cedar embedded or sidecar), a relationship store only when ReBAC needs it, and resource-specific checks still in services.
pts: In-process is fast but duplicated.
Local evaluation of centrally authored policies is a good default.
Central PDPs add latency and availability risk.
Relationship stores for ReBAC at scale.
Fail closed; test and stage policy bundles.
questions.ex: A bank's central PDP added 15 ms per call and became a single point of failure during an outage. Switching to OPA sidecars with centrally published bundles kept central governance while decisions took under 1 ms and survived PDP outages.

What are consistency tokens in OpenFGA?
How do you audit decisions?
pit: Network PDP call per request without caching or HA.

questions.q: Model corporate banking access with ReBAC (OpenFGA/Zanzibar style): companies, subsidiaries, accounts, users, roles and approval rights.
questions.a:
### Entities and relations
- **company**: {{admin}}, {{member}}, {{parent}} (subsidiary hierarchy).
- **account**: {{owner}} (a company), {{viewer}}, {{initiator}}, {{approver}} (users or company roles).
- Rights inherit: admins of a parent company can view subsidiaries' accounts if the model says so.

### Questions the model answers
- **Check**: can user U approve payments on account A?
- **List objects**: which accounts can U view? (for lists and dashboards)
- **Expand**: who can approve on account A? (for audits and approval routing)

### Writing relationships
Services write tuples when facts change (user assigned approver role, subsidiary added). Use the store as the source of truth for relationships, or sync from the system of record via events.

### Combine with ABAC
Amount thresholds, payment types and time windows are attributes; OpenFGA supports **conditions** (contextual tuples or CEL conditions), or evaluate thresholds in the service after the relationship check.

### Consistency
Use consistency tokens to avoid "new enemy" problems (a revoked user still allowed due to stale caches) for sensitive checks.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# OpenFGA authorization model (DSL)
model
  schema 1.1
type user
type company
  relations
    define parent: [company]
    define admin: [user] or admin from parent
    define member: [user] or admin
type account
  relations
    define owner: [company]
    define viewer: [user, company#member] or member from owner
    define initiator: [user, company#admin]
    define approver: [user with within_limit]
    define can_view: viewer or initiator or approver
    define can_initiate: initiator
    define can_approve: approver
condition within_limit(limit: double, amount: double) {
  amount <= limit
}
~~~
~~~csharp
// Check: can this user approve a 25,000 payment on this account?
var check = await fga.Check(new ClientCheckRequest
{
    User = $"user:{userId}", Relation = "can_approve", Object = $"account:{accountId}",
    Context = new { amount = 25_000.0 }
});
if (check.Allowed != true) return Results.NotFound();
~~~
pts: Relations for companies, hierarchies, accounts, users.
Check, list objects, expand.
Write tuples on facts; sync from systems of record.
Conditions for amount thresholds.
Consistency tokens for sensitive checks.
questions.ex: A corporate portal encoded subsidiary access in nested SQL joins that took 2 seconds for large groups and had inheritance bugs. An OpenFGA model with parent relations answered checks in 5 ms and list queries in 40 ms, and the expand API produced approval-right audits automatically.

List objects at scale?
What is the new enemy problem?

Putting thresholds in relations instead of conditions.

questions.q: What is SCIM, why does provisioning matter as much as authentication, and how do you implement a SCIM endpoint for your SaaS banking platform?
questions.a:
### The gap SSO leaves
SSO controls login, but accounts and entitlements inside the application persist after someone leaves unless they're **deprovisioned**. Just-in-time creation on first login doesn't remove access.

### SCIM 2.0
A REST standard ({{/Users}}, {{/Groups}}) for identity providers to create, update and deactivate users and group memberships in applications. Entra ID, Okta and others push changes automatically.

### Implementing a SCIM endpoint
- Endpoints: GET (filtering by {{userName eq}}), POST, PUT or PATCH (with SCIM patch operations), DELETE or {{active: false}}.
- Authentication: bearer token per customer tenant (or OAuth client credentials), scoped to that tenant.
- Map SCIM attributes to your user model; externalId to correlate.
- Groups to roles mapping configurable by the customer's admin.
- Deactivation revokes sessions and tokens immediately.
- Idempotency and conflict handling; audit every change.

### Testing
Microsoft's SCIM validator and Okta's test suites; edge cases (rename, re-hire, group removal).
pts: SSO doesn't deprovision; SCIM does.
Users and Groups endpoints with filters and patch.
Tenant-scoped SCIM credentials.
Deactivation revokes sessions immediately.
Validate with IdP test suites; audit changes.
questions.ex: A corporate client discovered that 40 ex-employees still had active users in a bank's cash management portal because only SSO was integrated. SCIM provisioning from the client's Entra ID now deactivates users within minutes of HR offboarding.

How do you map groups to roles?
How do you handle re-hires?
pit: Deactivation that waits for token expiry.

questions.q: Design the joiner-mover-leaver (JML) lifecycle for 20,000 employees and contractors. Why is the "mover" case where access risk accumulates?
questions.a:
### Source of truth
HR system (Workday, SAP SuccessFactors) for employees, a vendor management system for contractors. Identity governance (Entra ID Governance, SailPoint, Saviynt) consumes HR events.

### Joiner
Account created before day one with **birthright access** by role, department and location (email, collaboration, basic apps); additional access by request with approval; MFA enrolment at first login (Temporary Access Pass, not shared passwords).

### Mover
When someone changes job, the new role's birthright access is added but **old access is rarely removed**: privilege creep. Over years, long-tenured staff accumulate toxic combinations. Fix: on a mover event, recompute birthright access, flag non-birthright entitlements for review by the new manager within a deadline, auto-remove what isn't re-approved.

### Leaver
Disable at termination time (immediately for involuntary leavers), revoke sessions and tokens, remove from groups, reassign ownership of resources (mailboxes, service principals they own), deprovision downstream apps via SCIM, retain data per policy.

### Contractors
Expiry dates mandatory; sponsor accountable; auto-disable at end date.

### Measure
Time to disable leavers (minutes), orphaned accounts, mover access review completion, privilege creep indicators.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Lifecycle workflow (identity governance) triggered by HR events
workflows:
  - trigger: hr.employee.hired
    steps: [create-account, assign-birthright-by-attributes, issue-temporary-access-pass, notify-manager]
  - trigger: hr.employee.job_changed          # mover
    steps:
      - recompute-birthright
      - flag-non-birthright-entitlements: { reviewer: new-manager, deadline_days: 14, on_no_response: remove }
      - remove-old-department-groups: { grace_days: 7 }
  - trigger: hr.employee.terminated
    steps: [disable-account, revoke-sessions-and-refresh-tokens, remove-group-memberships, scim-deprovision-apps,
            transfer-owned-service-principals: { to: manager }, convert-mailbox-to-shared]
    sla_minutes: 15
  - trigger: contractor.end_date_reached
    steps: [disable-account, notify-sponsor]
~~~
pts: HR is the source of truth.
Birthright access by attributes; extra access by request.
Movers accumulate privilege: recompute and review.
Leavers disabled immediately with sessions revoked.
Contractor expiry and sponsors.
questions.ex: An audit found a payments operations analyst who had moved through four roles in six years still holding approval rights from all of them, including a toxic initiate-and-approve combination. Mover-triggered reviews removed 31% of non-birthright entitlements in the first quarter.

What is birthright access?
How do you handle shared accounts?
pit: Leavers disabled only at the next batch.

questions.q: Enforce segregation of duties and four-eyes approval for high-value payments in code and in data, so it cannot be bypassed by an admin or a direct API call.
questions.a:
### Rules
- The **initiator** cannot approve their own payment (and ideally not a payment initiated by someone they share a delegation with).
- High-value payments need **two distinct approvers** above thresholds.
- Approvers need the right entitlement and limits.
- Rules enforced in the **domain model and database**, not just the UI.

### Implementation
1. Domain aggregate tracks initiator and approvals; {{Approve}} rejects the initiator and duplicate approvers; state transitions require the configured number of approvals for the amount band.
2. Authorisation policy checks the approver's entitlement and limit.
3. Database constraint (unique approver per payment, check that approver differs from initiator) as defence in depth.
4. Step-up authentication for approval (transaction-bound).
5. Audit trail with both identities.
6. Admin and support tools use the same domain path; no direct table updates (permissions prevent them).

### SoD across roles
Toxic combinations (create vendor and pay vendor; change payee bank details and approve payment) detected in identity governance and prevented at role assignment time.
pts: Initiator can't approve; distinct approvers above thresholds.
Enforce in the domain model and database.
Entitlement and limit checks per approver.
Step-up for approval; full audit trail.
Prevent toxic role combinations at assignment.
questions.ex: A fraud investigation found an operator who approved his own payments through a support tool that updated the status column directly. Enforcing approval rules in the domain, removing direct table write permissions and adding database constraints made the bypass impossible.

questions.q: Design Entra ID app registrations for a web app calling three APIs. Explain app roles, delegated vs application permissions, scopes and consent, and common over-privilege mistakes.
questions.a:
### Concepts
- **App registration**: the application's identity definition (client id, redirect URIs, credentials, exposed scopes and app roles). **Enterprise application** (service principal): its instance in a tenant where users and permissions are assigned.
- **Delegated permissions (scopes)**: the app acts **on behalf of a signed-in user**; effective access is the intersection of the scope and the user's own rights.
- **Application permissions (app roles for apps)**: the app acts **as itself** (daemons, background jobs); no user; often powerful (for example Mail.Read across all mailboxes).
- **App roles for users**: roles assigned to users or groups, emitted in the {{roles}} claim.
- **Consent**: users or admins approve requested permissions; admin consent required for high-privilege permissions.

### Design for web app plus three APIs
Each API exposes scopes ({{api://payments/payments.read}}) and app roles; the web app requests only needed delegated scopes; background workers use separate registrations with minimal application permissions; managed identities instead of secrets where hosted in Azure.

### Over-privilege mistakes
Application permissions where delegated suffice, Graph permissions like {{Directory.ReadWrite.All}} granted "temporarily", one app registration shared by many services, client secrets with multi-year expiry, wildcard redirect URIs, and users allowed to consent to risky permissions (consent phishing).
pts: App registration vs enterprise application.
Delegated scopes act for users; application permissions act as the app.
App roles for users and apps.
Least privilege: delegated where possible, separate registrations.
Avoid broad Graph permissions, long secrets, wildcard redirects, user consent to risky scopes.
questions.ex: A reporting job was granted Directory.ReadWrite.All "to make it work"; when its client secret leaked, attackers could modify the directory. Replacing it with a managed identity holding only User.Read.All and restricting user consent closed both gaps.

questions.q: How do managed identities and workload identity federation remove secrets for workloads in Azure, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions and other clouds?
questions.a:
### Managed identities (Azure)
Azure issues tokens to resources (App Service, Functions, VMs, Container Apps, AKS pods via workload identity) through a local endpoint; no credential stored. System-assigned (lifecycle tied to the resource) or user-assigned (shared, pre-provisioned, survives redeployments).

### Workload identity federation
An external workload presents a **token from its own trusted issuer** (Kubernetes service account token, GitHub OIDC token, AWS or GCP identity) to Entra ID; a **federated credential** on an app registration or user-assigned identity trusts that issuer and **subject** (namespace and service account, repo and environment). Entra ID returns an access token. No secrets cross boundaries.

### AKS workload identity
1. Enable OIDC issuer and workload identity on the cluster.
2. Create a user-assigned managed identity with a federated credential for {{system:serviceaccount:payments:payments-api}}.
3. Annotate the service account with the identity's client id; pods using it get tokens via the Azure SDK ({{DefaultAzureCredential}}).

### Governance
One identity per workload, least-privilege role assignments scoped to specific resources, inventory of federated credentials (subjects must not be wildcards), alerts on unusual token use.

~~~yaml
# AKS workload identity: service account bound to a user-assigned managed identity
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    azure.workload.identity/client-id: "6f1c2d3e-4b5a-6978-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: payments-api, namespace: payments }
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { azure.workload.identity/use: "true" }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: payments-api
      containers: [{ name: app, image: "registry.bank.example/payments-api@sha256:7d2f..." }]
# Federated credential on the managed identity:
#   issuer:  https://westeurope.oic.prod-aks.azure.com/<tenant>/<cluster-guid>/
#   subject: system:serviceaccount:payments:payments-api
#   audience: api://AzureADTokenExchange
~~~
pts: Managed identities issue tokens to Azure resources without secrets.
Federation trusts external issuers by subject.
AKS workload identity binds service accounts to identities.
One identity per workload, least privilege.
No wildcard subjects; inventory and monitor.
questions.ex: A cluster used one service principal secret shared by 30 workloads stored as a Kubernetes secret; it leaked through a debug dump. Moving to workload identity with one managed identity per service removed the secret and limited each workload to its own Key Vault and database.

questions.q: Your tenant has 3,000 service principals, many with secrets. How do you assess and reduce the risk of non-human identities?
questions.a:
### Assess
Inventory: owner, purpose, credential type (secret, certificate, federated, managed identity), expiry, last sign-in, granted permissions (Graph application permissions, Azure RBAC roles, Key Vault access), whether multi-tenant, publisher verification for third-party apps.

### Risk signals
| Signal | Risk |
|---|---|
| secrets with long expiry or none | leak and persistence |
| high-privilege Graph permissions (Directory, Mail, Files across tenant) | tenant compromise |
| subscription Owner or Contributor | infrastructure takeover |
| no owner or owner departed | no accountability |
| unused for 90 days | dead weight attack surface |
| third-party multi-tenant apps with broad consent | supply chain and consent phishing |

### Reduce
1. Remove unused identities and permissions (start with no sign-ins in 90 days).
2. Migrate to managed identities or workload identity federation; certificates (short-lived, in Key Vault) where secrets remain.
3. Right-size permissions: scope roles to resource groups or resources, replace broad Graph permissions with narrower ones or resource-specific consent.
4. Owners required; periodic reviews of non-human identities like human access reviews.
5. Policies: restrict who can create app registrations, block user consent to high-risk permissions, credential lifetime limits (app management policies).
6. Monitor service principal sign-ins and anomalous token use (workload identity protection).

  | jq -r '.value[] | select((.passwordCredentials | length) > 0) | [.displayName, .appId, ([.passwordCredentials[].endDateTime] | max)] | @tsv' \
  | sort -t$'\t' -k3 > sp-secrets.tsv

az rest --method GET --url "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals?\$filter=appId eq '00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000'&\$expand=appRoleAssignedTo" \

~~~

Remove unused identities first.
Move to managed identities and federation; certificates otherwise.
Scope permissions narrowly; owners and reviews.
Policies on creation, consent and credential lifetimes; monitor sign-ins.

questions.q: Design conditional access policies for a bank's workforce. Which signals do you use, and how do you avoid lockouts and policy sprawl?
questions.a:
### Signals
User and group, application, device state (compliant via Intune, hybrid joined), location (named locations, countries), client app type, sign-in risk and user risk (identity protection), authentication strength, session context.

### Baseline policies
| Policy | Effect |
|---|---|
| Require MFA for all users | baseline |
| **Phishing-resistant authentication strength** for admins and privileged roles | FIDO2, Windows Hello, certificate-based |
| Require compliant or hybrid-joined device for sensitive apps (core banking, payments ops) | no access from unmanaged devices |
| Block legacy authentication | removes password-only protocols |
| Block or require step-up for high sign-in risk | stops credential stuffing and token replay patterns |
| Restrict access by country for sensitive roles | reduce attack surface |
| Session controls: sign-in frequency, no persistent browser on unmanaged devices | limit token lifetime exposure |
| Token protection (binding) where supported | reduce token theft value |

### Avoiding lockouts and sprawl
- **Emergency access accounts** excluded from policies, monitored, with FIDO2 keys stored securely.
- Report-only mode before enforcement; What If tool.
- Naming conventions, policy as code (Graph API, Terraform), change review.
- Persona-based design (standard users, admins, developers, guests, service accounts) instead of one-off policies.
pts: Signals: user, app, device, location, risk, auth strength.
Baseline MFA, phishing-resistant for privileged.
Compliant devices for sensitive apps; block legacy auth.
Emergency accounts excluded and monitored.
Report-only first; personas; policies as code.
questions.ex: A policy change requiring compliant devices was enabled directly and locked out the whole operations team using new laptops not yet enrolled. Report-only rollouts with What If checks and emergency accounts prevented a repeat during the next change.
fu: What is authentication strength?
How do you handle guests?
What is token protection?
pit: Dozens of overlapping ad hoc policies.

questions.q: How long should sessions and tokens live, and how do you revoke access quickly when an account is compromised or a user leaves?
questions.a:
### The trade-off
Short-lived tokens limit exposure but increase refreshes; long-lived tokens improve UX but delay revocation. JWT access tokens can't be "taken back" before expiry without extra mechanisms.

### Typical settings
| Artifact | Lifetime |
|---|---|
| access token | 5 to 60 minutes (Entra ID default about 60 to 90) |
| refresh token | rolling, hours to 90 days, **revocable**, rotated on use (public clients) |
| web session cookie | idle timeout 15 to 30 minutes for banking; absolute timeout hours |
| step-up assertion | minutes, for the specific transaction |

### Revocation mechanisms
- **Revoke refresh tokens and sessions** at the IdP (user disable, password reset, admin revoke).
- **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)**: resource providers that support CAE (Microsoft Graph, Exchange, and your APIs via claims challenges) receive critical events (user disabled, high risk, location change) and reject tokens in near real time; CAE-enabled tokens may live longer (up to 28 hours) because revocation is event-driven.
- For your own APIs: short access token lifetimes plus a **revocation check** for sensitive operations (session id or user status lookup, cached briefly), or token introspection for high-risk endpoints.
- Application sessions: server-side session store you can delete.

### Leaver or compromise runbook
Disable account, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, reset credentials and MFA methods, check for persistence (new MFA methods, OAuth consents, mailbox rules, app credentials), and review recent activity.
pts: Short access tokens; revocable rotating refresh tokens.
Idle and absolute session timeouts for banking.
CAE delivers near-real-time revocation events.
Revocation checks for sensitive operations.
Compromise runbook covers persistence.
questions.ex: A terminated employee kept using a cash management portal for 50 minutes because the portal trusted a 60-minute access token and had no revocation check. Adding a cached session-status check on sensitive operations, fed by IdP events, cut the exposure window to under a minute.
fu: How does CAE work with custom APIs?
What does refresh token rotation detect?
Is token introspection worth its latency?
pit: No idle timeout for banking sessions.

questions.q: Design identity for a multi-tenant B2B SaaS treasury platform used by hundreds of corporate clients, each with their own IdP and admins.
questions.a:
### Requirements
Each client: federate with their own IdP (Entra ID, Okta, ADFS via SAML or OIDC) or use platform-managed accounts; their admins manage users and roles; strict tenant isolation; SCIM provisioning; MFA policies per client but with platform minimums.

### Architecture
- **Identity broker** (Entra External ID, Auth0 Organizations, Duende with per-tenant IdPs): home realm discovery by email domain or tenant subdomain, per-tenant IdP configuration, issues platform tokens with a {{tenant_id}} claim.
- **Tenant isolation**: tenant id from the token only; every query scoped (RLS); per-tenant encryption keys optional.
- **Delegated administration**: client admins manage their users, roles and approval matrices in a tenant admin portal; platform staff have separate, audited, JIT support access.
- **Provisioning**: SCIM per tenant; JIT provisioning with default minimal role as fallback.
- **Policies**: platform minimum (MFA required, session limits), clients can strengthen (IP allow-lists, phishing-resistant MFA).

### Pitfalls
Trusting email domains for tenant mapping without verification, users belonging to multiple tenants (support explicit tenant switching), and platform admins with standing cross-tenant access.
pts: Identity broker with per-tenant IdP federation.
Tenant id only from tokens; queries scoped.
Delegated admin for clients; JIT for platform staff.
SCIM per tenant; platform minimum policies.
Verify domains; support explicit multi-tenant users.
questions.ex: A treasury SaaS mapped tenants from an email domain in a header; a tester changed it and saw another corporate client's cash positions. Resolving the tenant only from broker-issued tokens, with RLS in the database, closed the gap.
fu: How do you handle users in multiple tenants?
How do client admins define approval matrices?
What does home realm discovery need?
pit: Standing platform admin access to all tenants.

questions.q: Design just-in-time privileged access for Azure, Kubernetes and databases using PIM and groups. How do you keep on-call engineers effective?
questions.a:
### Model
- **No permanent privileged role assignments** in production (except break-glass).
- **PIM for Groups**: eligible membership in privileged groups (for example {{pim-payments-prod-contributor}}); the group holds Azure RBAC roles, Kubernetes RBAC bindings (via Entra groups), and database roles (Entra-authenticated SQL users mapped to groups).
- Activation requires phishing-resistant MFA, justification, ticket or incident id, and approval for the most sensitive roles; time-boxed (1 to 8 hours).

### On-call effectiveness
- Self-approval-free but **fast** activation for read and operate roles during incidents (pre-approved for on-call rotation members, still logged).
- Approval required for data access and destructive roles.
- Runbooks automated (GitOps, pipelines) so humans rarely need write access.
- Read-only access to logs and metrics without elevation.

### Monitoring and review
Alerts on activations outside on-call or change windows, on break-glass use, and on direct role assignments bypassing PIM; quarterly reviews of eligibility.

# Terraform: privileged group with PIM eligibility, mapped to Azure and AKS roles

  display_name       = "pim-payments-prod-operator"
  security_enabled   = true
  assignable_to_role = true
}

  scope                = azurerm_kubernetes_cluster.prod.id
  role_definition_name = "Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Writer"

PIM for Groups maps to Azure, Kubernetes and database roles.
MFA, justification, ticket, time limits; approval for sensitive roles.
Fast pre-approved activation for on-call operate roles.
Alerts on unusual activations and direct assignments.
questions.ex: Production had 180 permanent Contributor assignments; after an engineer's laptop compromise, the attacker had immediate infrastructure access. Moving to PIM groups with 4-hour activations reduced standing privileged accounts to the break-glass pair.

questions.q: Access reviews are rubber-stamped: managers approve 99.8% of access. How do you make certification meaningful?
questions.a:
### Why rubber-stamping happens
Reviewers see hundreds of cryptic entitlements ({{GRP-APP-0419-RW}}), no usage data, no risk context, and a deadline; approving everything is the rational choice.

### Make reviews meaningful
| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Business-friendly descriptions** of entitlements (what it allows, risk level, data sensitivity) | reviewers understand |
| **Usage data**: last used date, recommendations ("not used in 90 days: remove") | evidence-based decisions |
| **Risk-based scope**: review privileged, sensitive and toxic combinations more often; low-risk birthright access less (or not at all) | smaller, focused reviews |
| **Right reviewer**: resource owners for application entitlements, managers for people context | accountability |
| **Defaults**: auto-remove on no response for high-risk access | removes passive approvals |
| **Micro-certifications**: event-driven reviews on mover events or anomalies | timely |
| Measure revocation rates and spot-check approvals | detect rubber stamps |

### Automate where possible
Remove dormant access automatically (no sign-in for 90 days), expire temporary grants, and enforce SoD rules at request time so reviews aren't the only control.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Access review definition (identity governance), risk-based
review:
  name: payments-privileged-quarterly
  scope:
    entitlements: [tag:privileged, tag:payments, tag:customer-data]
    include_toxic_combinations: true
  reviewers:
    application_entitlements: resource-owner
    people_context: manager
  context_shown: [entitlement-description, risk-level, last-used, peer-comparison, recommendation]
  recommendations:
    not_used_days: 90                  # recommend deny
  on_no_response: remove               # for privileged scope
  frequency: quarterly
  quality_controls:
    flag_reviewer_if_approve_rate_over: 0.98
    sample_audit_pct: 5
---
dormant_access_policy: { remove_after_days_unused: 90, notify_owner_days_before: 14 }
~~~
pts: Cryptic lists and no context cause rubber stamps.
Descriptions, usage data and recommendations.
Risk-based scope and right reviewers.
Auto-remove on no response for high risk.
Automate dormant removal; enforce SoD at request time.
questions.ex: Quarterly reviews of 40,000 entitlements removed 0.2% of access. After adding last-used data, recommendations and resource-owner reviews for privileged entitlements only, removals rose to 18% of reviewed access while review volume fell by 70%.

questions.q: Design the entitlement model for a bank's internal operations platform used by 4,000 staff across 30 functions. How do you keep it understandable and auditable?
questions.a:
### Layers
1. **Permissions** (fine-grained, owned by applications): {{payments.view}}, {{payments.release}}, {{customer.contact.update}}, {{limits.change}}. Defined in code or manifests, versioned.
2. **Roles** (business-meaningful bundles): "Payments Operations Analyst" = view, investigate, return; "Payments Releaser" = release up to limit. Owned by business owners.
3. **Constraints** (attributes): region, branch, product line, approval limits, data classification.
4. **Assignments**: users or groups to roles, via access requests with approval, time-bound where appropriate.

### Principles
- Applications check **permissions** (capabilities), never role names: role restructuring doesn't need code changes.
- Each permission has an owner, description, risk level and data classification.
- SoD rules expressed on permissions (release and initiate conflict).
- One **entitlement catalogue** feeds access requests, reviews and audits.
- Keep roles few and stable (tens, not thousands); use constraints instead of new roles.

### Delivery to apps
Coarse roles in tokens; permissions and constraints from an entitlement service (cached), or compiled into tokens for short-lived internal tokens via token exchange.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Entitlement catalogue (source of truth, versioned)
permissions:
  - id: payments.release
    app: payments-ops
    description: "Release a held payment to the scheme"
    risk: high
    data: [payment, customer-financial]
    sod_conflicts: [payments.initiate, payee.bank_details.update]
  - id: payments.view
    app: payments-ops
    description: "View payments and their status"
    risk: medium
roles:
  - id: payments-releaser
    owner: head-of-payments-operations
    permissions: [payments.view, payments.release]
    constraints: { approval_limit: { max: 250000 }, regions: [UK, EU] }
    assignment: { requires_approval: [manager, role-owner], max_duration_days: 365, review: quarterly }
~~~
~~~csharp
// Apps check permissions, never role names
app.MapPost("/payments/{id:guid}/release", Release).RequireAuthorization(p => p.RequireClaim("perm", "payments.release"));
~~~
pts: Permissions owned by apps; roles owned by business.
Constraints instead of role explosion.
Apps check permissions, not role names.
Catalogue with owners, risk, SoD conflicts.
Few stable roles; reviews driven by risk.
questions.ex: An operations platform had permissions embedded as role-name checks in 300 places; reorganising teams required code changes in 12 services. Moving to permission checks and a catalogue let the business restructure roles without any deployment.

questions.q: Authorisation checks add 30 ms to every request and fail when the entitlement service is slow. How do you make authorisation fast and resilient without making it stale or unsafe?
questions.a:
### Options
| Technique | Effect | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Local evaluation** of policies (OPA or Cedar embedded, ASP.NET Core handlers) | sub-ms decisions | policy distribution |
| **Cache entitlements per user** (short TTL, event-driven invalidation) | removes lookups | staleness after revocation |
| Put **coarse** entitlements in tokens; look up **fine** ones only for sensitive operations | fewer lookups | token staleness |
| Batch checks (check many resources at once, list-objects APIs) | fewer round trips | API support |
| Precompute decisions into read models (who can see which accounts) | fast lists | sync complexity |

### Staleness and safety
- Revocations must propagate quickly: subscribe to entitlement change events and evict caches; short TTLs (1 to 5 minutes) as backstop.
- **Sensitive operations** (payments release, limit changes) bypass caches or use consistency tokens.
- **Fail closed** on errors for sensitive operations; for low-risk reads, serving from a recent cache during an outage may be an explicit, documented choice.

### Measure
Authorisation latency as its own span; cache hit rate; propagation time for revocations (test it).
pts: Evaluate policies locally.
Cache entitlements with event-driven invalidation.
Coarse in tokens, fine-grained lookups when sensitive.
Fresh or consistent checks for sensitive operations.
Fail closed for sensitive operations; measure revocation propagation.
questions.ex: Every request called an entitlement API (30 ms p50, 400 ms p99). A 2-minute cache with change-event eviction, plus fresh checks only for release and limit changes, cut authorisation overhead to under 1 ms for 97% of requests while revocations propagated in under 10 seconds.
fu: How do you test revocation propagation?
What TTL is acceptable?
How do list endpoints authorise efficiently?
pit: Remote call per request without caching.

questions.q: Support agents need to see what a customer sees to help them. Design customer impersonation or "view as" safely.
questions.a:
### Risks
Agents abusing access (curiosity, fraud), actions taken in the customer's name, unclear audit trails, and support tools becoming the easiest path to customer data.

### Design
- **Never log in as the customer**: no shared credentials, no password resets for convenience.
- **Act-as with dual identity**: tokens carry both the **actor** (agent) and the **subject** (customer) (OAuth token exchange {{act}} claim); every downstream service sees both.
- **Read-only by default**: "view as" shows the customer's screens without write capabilities; specific assisted actions (resend card PIN letter) are separate, audited operations with their own permissions.
- **Consent and reason**: customer consent captured (phone verification, in-app approval) or a case id required; time-boxed session (15 to 30 minutes).
- **Data minimisation**: masked sensitive fields unless needed.
- **Audit**: who, which customer, why, what was viewed or done; customer-visible access history where appropriate.
- **Monitoring**: unusual volumes of impersonation sessions, sessions on VIPs or employees' own family accounts.
pts: Never log in as the customer.
Act-as tokens carry actor and subject.
Read-only by default; assisted actions separately permitted.
Consent or case id, time-boxed sessions, masking.
Audit and monitor impersonation.
questions.ex: A support tool let agents reset customers' passwords and log in as them; an insider used it to redirect payments. Replacing it with act-as tokens, read-only masked views and case-linked sessions removed the attack path and created a complete audit trail.
fu: How does OAuth token exchange represent actors?
Should customers see access history?
What assisted actions are acceptable?

questions.q: Design customer identity for a digital bank: registration bound to KYC, credential setup, device binding, account linking and recovery.
questions.a:
### Registration
1. Collect minimal data; run **identity verification** (document plus liveness, or bank-ID schemes) and sanctions screening.
2. Create the customer record and **identity account** only after KYC passes (or in a restricted state).
3. Bind credentials: passkey on the device, or app with device-bound keys (secure enclave) unlocked by biometrics.

### Identifiers
Internal immutable subject id (never the email or phone); email and phone as verified attributes that can change.

### Account linking
Customers with existing products (credit card, mortgage) are linked to the new identity after strong verification (matching KYC data plus a one-time code to a channel on file); never auto-link by email alone.

### Recovery
Recovery is the attack path: new device enrolment requires re-verification (document plus liveness or an existing trusted device), cooling-off periods before high-risk actions, notifications on all channels.

### Platform
CIAM product (Entra External ID, Okta CIC, Ping) or a self-hosted identity server (Duende) integrated with KYC providers; risk engine and fraud signals at each step; consent management (marketing, open banking).
questions.dia:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Mobile app
  participant I as Identity service
  participant K as KYC provider
  participant C as Core banking
  A->>I: start registration (email, phone)
  I->>K: document + liveness session
  K-->>I: verified identity attributes
  I->>C: create customer (KYC passed)
  C-->>I: customer id
  I->>A: register passkey / device key
  A-->>I: public key + attestation
  I-->>A: tokens for customer id
pts: Registration bound to KYC; identity created after verification.
Immutable internal subject ids.
Device-bound keys or passkeys.
Account linking only with strong verification.
Recovery with re-verification and cooling-off.
questions.ex: A bank auto-linked new app registrations to existing card accounts by matching email; fraudsters registered with victims' emails from breached lists and took over cards. Linking now requires KYC matching plus a one-time code to the phone on file.

What if KYC data changes?

questions.q: Corporate clients define approval matrices ("payments over 100k need one A and one B signatory"). Model mandates and enforce them correctly.
questions.a:
### Mandate model
- **Signatory groups** (A, B, C) assigned to client users by the client's administrators (with bank verification for signatory changes).
- **Rules** per account or account group, payment type and amount band: for example under 10k: any one of A or B; 10k to 100k: two signatures (any groups); over 100k: one A and one B.
- **Validity** dates, currency, beneficiary types (new beneficiaries require stricter rules).

### Enforcement
1. When a payment is submitted, resolve the applicable rule (account, type, amount, currency).
2. Collect approvals: each approval records the signatory, groups at that time, and the step-up authentication.
3. Evaluate whether the set of approvals satisfies the rule (combinatorial: assign approvers to required slots).
4. Initiator rules: can an initiator also sign? Configurable per client (often not).
5. Rule changes require dual control by client admins and bank-side verification.

### Edge cases
Signatory removed after approving (approval valid if they were authorised at the time; policy decision), multi-currency thresholds (convert at a defined rate), batch payments (rule applies per payment or per batch total; define clearly).
pts: Signatory groups, rules by account, type, amount, validity.
Record groups at approval time.
Evaluate rule satisfaction as slot assignment.
Configurable initiator rules.
Dual control for mandate changes; define edge cases.
questions.ex: A cash management platform checked "two approvals" but not that they came from groups A and B; a client's two B signatories released a 2M payment that required an A signatory. Slot-based evaluation and tests for each mandate shape fixed it.
fu: How do you handle batch payment files?
What if a signatory leaves mid-approval?
How do clients change mandates securely?
pit: Not recording groups at approval time.

questions.q: How should user identity propagate through a chain of microservices? Compare forwarding tokens, token exchange, and internal tokens, including audit and least privilege.
questions.a:
### Options
| Option | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Forward the user's access token** | each service validates the same token | simple, end-to-end user context | token audience must include many services (broad), replay risk inside the network |
| **Token exchange** (RFC 8693, Entra on-behalf-of) | each hop exchanges the incoming token for one scoped to the next service's audience | least privilege per hop, actor chain recorded | STS calls (cache), latency |
| **Internal signed tokens** minted at the edge | gateway issues short-lived internal JWT with selected claims | uniform internal format, small tokens | gateway holds signing keys; trust concentrated |
| **Service identity only** (mTLS, client credentials) plus user id as data | services trust the caller service, user id passed as a parameter | simple | user context not cryptographically bound: confused deputy risk |

### Recommendations
Token exchange (or on-behalf-of) for user-context calls to sensitive services; service identity for system-to-system calls without a user; never pass user ids as trusted plain headers; record the full actor chain in audit logs.

### Confused deputy
A service acting with its own broad privileges on behalf of any user can be tricked into accessing data the user shouldn't see; bound user context (exchanged tokens) prevents that.
pts: Forwarding is simple but broad.
Token exchange scopes each hop and records actors.
Internal tokens concentrate trust at the gateway.
Service identity alone risks confused deputies.
Never trust plain user-id headers; audit the actor chain.
questions.ex: A reporting service used its own broad database identity and a userId query parameter; a user changed the parameter and pulled another customer's statements. Switching to on-behalf-of tokens with the user's identity enforced at the data service closed the confused-deputy hole.
fu: How do you cache exchanged tokens?
What about async flows through Kafka?
How does the act claim work?
pit: Tokens with audiences for every service.
Broad service identities acting for users.

questions.q: How do you test authorisation thoroughly: unit tests for policies, matrix tests for endpoints, and regression tests when roles change?
questions.a:
### Layers
| Test type | What it proves |
|---|---|
| **Policy unit tests** (OPA {{opa test}}, Cedar tests, handler tests) | each rule allows and denies expected inputs |
| **Endpoint permission matrix** | every endpoint x role or persona returns the expected status (200, 403, 404) |
| **BOLA tests** | user A can't access user B's resources across all id-taking endpoints |
| **Tenant isolation tests** | cross-tenant requests fail, including list endpoints |
| **SoD tests** | initiator can't approve; toxic combinations rejected |
| **Revocation tests** | access removed propagates within the target time |
| **Snapshot of effective permissions** | role changes produce reviewed diffs ("who can release payments" before and after) |

### Practices
- Generate the matrix from route metadata so new endpoints are automatically included (test fails if an endpoint has no expectation).
- Personas with realistic claims, generated tokens from a test issuer.
- Run in CI; failing expectation changes need security review.
pts: Unit-test policies and handlers.
Endpoint by persona matrix with expected statuses.
BOLA, tenant, SoD and revocation tests.
Matrix coverage enforced for new endpoints.
Effective permission diffs reviewed.
questions.ex: A refactor moved an endpoint to a new controller and lost its policy attribute; the fallback policy allowed any authenticated user. The permission matrix test caught it in CI because the ops-analyst persona suddenly got 200 instead of 403.
fu: How do you generate realistic test tokens?
How do you test OPA bundles?
How do you keep the matrix maintainable?
pit: No coverage check for new endpoints.

questions.q: Regulators ask: "Who accessed this customer's data in the last year, and why were they allowed?" Design authorisation decision auditing that can answer it.
questions.a:
### What to record
For sensitive resources (customer data, payments, limits):
- **Who**: subject, actor (if acting on behalf), client app, authentication method and strength, session id.
- **What**: action, resource type and id (customer id), fields or data classes accessed.
- **Decision**: allow or deny, policy and version that decided, key attributes used (role, relationship, branch), reason or case id.
- **When and where**: timestamp from a trusted clock, source IP, device, service.

### Pipeline
Structured audit events emitted by the authorisation layer (handler or PDP), delivered reliably (outbox, not sampled logs), stored immutably with retention, indexed by resource and subject for queries.

### Answering the question
Query by customer id: list of access events with subjects and decisions; join with entitlement history (who held which role when) to explain "why allowed". Store **policy version** so decisions can be reproduced.

### Volume
High-volume reads may be aggregated (one event per session per customer per action type) rather than per request, while writes and sensitive actions are always individually recorded.
pts: Record who, actor, what, decision, policy version, inputs, when.
Reliable delivery to immutable storage.
Index by resource and subject.
Join with entitlement history to explain why.
Aggregate high-volume reads; always record sensitive actions.
questions.ex: A regulator asked who had viewed a high-profile customer's account; logs held only HTTP access lines without user identities for internal tools. After adding authorisation decision events, the next such request was answered in minutes with names, roles and case references.
fu: How long do you retain decision logs?

questions.q: Migrate a bank from on-premises Active Directory (with ADFS, Kerberos apps and LDAP) to Entra ID. What is the plan and what are the traps?
questions.a:
### Phases
1. **Hybrid identity**: Entra Connect (or Cloud Sync) synchronises users and groups; choose authentication: **password hash sync** (resilient, enables leaked credential detection) with seamless SSO, or pass-through authentication; plan to retire ADFS.
2. **Apps to Entra ID**: move SAML and WS-Fed apps from ADFS to Entra ID enterprise apps (ADFS application activity report helps); modern apps to OIDC.
3. **Legacy protocols**: Kerberos and header-based apps via **Entra Application Proxy** or Private Access; LDAP apps via Entra Domain Services or modernise; NTLM elimination plan.
4. **Devices**: hybrid join then Entra join with Intune; conditional access on device compliance.
5. **Privileged access**: tier 0 (domain controllers, Entra Connect servers) protected; cloud-only admin accounts with phishing-resistant MFA, not synced admins.
6. **Decommission** ADFS; reduce AD footprint over time.

### Traps
- Synced on-prem admins becoming cloud global admins (on-prem compromise equals cloud compromise).
- Entra Connect server treated as an ordinary server (it is tier 0).
- Service accounts with passwords never rotated, SPNs with weak encryption (Kerberoasting).
- Apps hard-coded to UPN formats or group names.
- Underestimating the long tail of legacy apps.

~~~powershell
# Inventory ADFS relying parties and their usage before migration (on the ADFS server)
Get-AdfsRelyingPartyTrust | Select-Object Name, Identifier, Enabled, IssuanceAuthorizationRules |
  Export-Csv adfs-relying-parties.csv -NoTypeInformation

# Find accounts with SPNs (Kerberoasting exposure) and old passwords
Get-ADUser -Filter 'ServicePrincipalName -like "*"' -Properties ServicePrincipalName, PasswordLastSet, msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes |
  Select-Object SamAccountName, PasswordLastSet, @{n='SPNs';e={$_.ServicePrincipalName -join ';'}}, msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes |
  Sort-Object PasswordLastSet | Export-Csv spn-accounts.csv -NoTypeInformation

# Cloud-only break-glass and admin accounts: never synced from on-prem
# Entra: Global Administrator assignments must be cloud-only identities with FIDO2 keys
~~~
pts: Hybrid sync with password hash sync; retire ADFS.
Move SAML/WS-Fed apps; Application Proxy for Kerberos apps.
Devices to Entra join and Intune.
Cloud-only privileged accounts; Entra Connect is tier 0.
Inventory the legacy long tail; fix service account hygiene.
questions.ex: A ransomware group that compromised on-prem AD at a financial firm also controlled Microsoft 365 because synced domain admins held Global Administrator. The bank's migration plan made all cloud admins cloud-only with FIDO2 keys and isolated the Entra Connect server as tier 0.

questions.q: Modern identity attacks bypass MFA: adversary-in-the-middle phishing, token theft, MFA fatigue, consent phishing, device code abuse. How do you defend against each?
questions.a:
| Attack | How | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| **AiTM phishing** (Evilginx-style reverse proxies) | proxy captures password, MFA and the resulting session cookie | **phishing-resistant MFA** (FIDO2, passkeys, Windows Hello, CBA) bound to origin; token protection; conditional access with compliant devices |
| **Token or cookie theft** (infostealer malware) | stolen refresh tokens or session cookies replayed | token binding (token protection, DPoP), device compliance, short sessions, CAE and risk-based revocation, EDR |
| **MFA fatigue** (push bombing) | spam push approvals until the user accepts | number matching, additional context, rate limits on prompts, phishing-resistant methods |
| **Consent phishing** | malicious OAuth app asks for mailbox or file permissions | restrict user consent (verified publishers, low-risk permissions only), admin consent workflow, app governance |
| **Device code phishing** | attacker starts device code flow, tricks user into entering the code | block device code flow except where needed (conditional access authentication flows) |
| **SIM swap** | takes over SMS OTP | avoid SMS for sensitive roles |
| **Password spray** | common passwords across many accounts | smart lockout, banned passwords, MFA, block legacy auth |

### Detection
Identity protection risk signals, impossible travel, new MFA method registration followed by sensitive actions, unusual OAuth consents, token replay from new IPs or ASNs.
pts: Phishing-resistant MFA defeats AiTM.
Bind tokens and require compliant devices against theft.
Number matching against MFA fatigue.
Restrict user consent; app governance.
Block device code flow where unused; detect risky patterns.
questions.ex: An AiTM phishing campaign captured session cookies of 12 finance staff despite push MFA; attackers changed vendor bank details. After enforcing FIDO2 for finance roles and compliant-device conditional access, the same kit failed: keys refused to sign for the attacker's domain.

pit: Allowing users to consent to any app.
Leaving device code flow open to everyone.

questions.q: Detect and prevent toxic access combinations across many systems (core banking, payments, ERP, vendor management). How do you build SoD controls that work across applications?
questions.a:
### Problem
Each system enforces its own roles, but fraud often spans systems: create a vendor in the ERP, change bank details in vendor management, approve payment in the payments platform. No single system sees the combination.

### Approach
1. **Entitlement catalogue** across systems with normalised permission names and risk tags.
2. **SoD rule set** defined by risk and compliance: pairs or sets of permissions that must not coexist ({{vendor.create}} + {{payment.approve}}), with scope (same entity, same region).
3. **Preventive control**: access request workflow checks SoD before granting; conflicts require compensating control approval (documented, time-boxed) or are blocked.
4. **Detective control**: periodic analysis of actual assignments (identity governance platform) and of **activity** (did the same person perform both steps on the same transaction?).
5. **Transactional enforcement** in apps where possible (initiator cannot approve), which catches what role analysis misses.

### Operations
Conflicts dashboard per business area, owners for each rule, mitigations tracked, and reporting to risk committees and auditors.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Cross-system SoD rules (identity governance)
sod_rules:
  - id: SOD-P2P-01
    description: "Create vendor and approve vendor payments"
    conflict: [erp.vendor.create, payments.vendor_payment.approve]
    scope: same-legal-entity
    severity: critical
    action_on_request: block
  - id: SOD-P2P-02
    description: "Change payee bank details and release payments"
    conflict: [vendor_mgmt.bank_details.update, payments.release]
    severity: high
    action_on_request: require-compensating-control
    compensating_controls: [daily review of bank detail changes by finance control, dual release above 10k]
detective:
  assignments_scan: daily
  activity_scan:
    rule: "same user performed vendor.bank_details.update and payments.release on same vendor within 30 days"
    destination: siem
~~~
pts: Fraud spans systems; single-app SoD misses it.
Cross-system catalogue and SoD rules.
Prevent at request time; compensating controls when needed.
Detect from assignments and actual activity.
Transactional enforcement inside apps.
questions.ex: An internal fraud used legitimate access in three systems: the employee created a shell vendor, updated its bank details and released payments. Cross-system SoD rules flagged 41 similar conflicting assignments; activity scanning now alerts on the sequence within a day.

questions.q: Design emergency access for when the identity provider, MFA service or conditional access misconfiguration locks everyone out.
questions.a:
### Break-glass accounts
- Two or more **cloud-only** accounts (not synced from on-prem), Global Administrator, excluded from conditional access policies that could lock them out, protected with **FIDO2 keys** stored in separate physical safes, long random passwords split between custodians where used.
- No mailbox or daily use; monitored: any sign-in alerts the security team immediately.
- Tested quarterly (sign-in drill) with documented procedure.

### Scenarios
| Scenario | Response |
|---|---|
| conditional access policy locks out admins | break-glass sign-in, fix or disable policy |
| MFA provider outage | break-glass, temporary policy adjustments with logging; avoid disabling MFA broadly |
| Entra ID regional outage | rely on resilience defaults (backup authentication service), pre-issued tokens; applications degrade gracefully |
| on-prem AD compromise | cloud-only admins unaffected; isolate sync |
| application IdP (customer CIAM) outage | existing sessions continue; plan for degraded login and status communication |

### Applications
Apps should tolerate brief IdP unavailability: cached signing keys (JWKS), existing sessions remain valid, token refresh retries with backoff, and clear user messaging.
pts: Cloud-only break-glass accounts with FIDO2 keys in safes.
Excluded from risky policies; monitored and drilled.
Playbooks per lockout scenario.
Don't disable MFA broadly during outages.
Apps tolerate brief IdP outages with cached keys and sessions.
questions.ex: A conditional access change requiring compliant devices for all admins locked out the identity team for 3 hours because the only break-glass account had been included and its password was unknown. Two properly excluded, monitored FIDO2 break-glass accounts and quarterly drills now exist.

questions.q: Your organisation has 9,000 roles for 6,000 users. How do you rationalise roles using role mining without breaking people's work?
questions.a:
### Diagnose
Roles created per request, per person, per team variation; many roles with one member; nested groups; overlapping roles differing by one permission.

### Role mining
Analyse actual assignments (and ideally **usage**) to find clusters: users in the same job function sharing permission sets. Algorithms (clustering, frequent itemsets) propose candidate roles; business owners validate.

### Rationalisation plan
1. **Define job-function roles** with business owners (top-down) informed by mined clusters (bottom-up).
2. **Move context out of roles** into attributes (region, branch, limits).
3. **Map** existing assignments to new roles; identify residual permissions (exceptions) per user.
4. **Run in parallel**: grant new roles, monitor access denials, then remove old roles in waves.
5. **Remove unused** permissions (not used in 90 days) during the migration.
6. **Governance**: new role creation requires justification, owner and review; role metrics (members, permissions, overlap) monitored.

### Success
Fewer roles (hundreds), higher review quality, faster onboarding, fewer SoD conflicts.
questions.code:
~~~sql
-- Candidate role discovery: permission sets shared by many users in the same job family
WITH user_perms AS (
    SELECT u.UserId, u.JobFamily, STRING_AGG(CAST(p.PermissionId AS NVARCHAR(MAX)), ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY p.PermissionId) AS PermSet
    FROM iam.Users u
    JOIN iam.EffectivePermissions p ON p.UserId = u.UserId
    WHERE p.LastUsedAt >= DATEADD(day, -90, SYSUTCDATETIME())          -- only permissions actually used
    GROUP BY u.UserId, u.JobFamily
)
SELECT JobFamily, PermSet, COUNT(*) AS Users
FROM user_perms
GROUP BY JobFamily, PermSet
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10
ORDER BY JobFamily, Users DESC;
~~~
pts: Role explosion from per-request and per-person roles.
Mine actual assignments and usage for clusters.
Business-owned job-function roles plus attributes.
Parallel run, monitor denials, remove in waves.
Govern new roles with owners and metrics.
questions.ex: A bank rationalised 9,200 roles to 380 job-function roles plus attributes over 9 months; access review effort fell by 75% and new joiners got correct access on day one instead of after two weeks of tickets.

questions.q: ABAC policies are only as good as their attributes. Where do subject, resource and environment attributes come from, and how do you handle freshness and trust?
questions.a:
### Attribute sources
| Attribute | Source | Freshness concern |
|---|---|---|
| job function, department, branch, grade | HR system via identity governance | job changes propagate with delay |
| approval limits, certifications | entitlement system, training system | expiry dates |
| clearance, risk flags (under investigation) | security or HR case systems | must apply immediately |
| resource classification, owner, region | application data, data catalogue | must be correct at creation |
| device compliance, location, risk | IdP and conditional access, endpoint management | per sign-in or continuous |
| time, network zone | request context | real time |

### Trust and integrity
Attributes in tokens are only as trustworthy as their issuer and as fresh as the token; high-impact attributes (limits, investigation flags) should be fetched from authoritative sources at decision time (cached briefly with invalidation). Resource attributes must be set by systems, not users.

### Data quality
Missing attributes default to **deny**; attribute coverage dashboards; owners per attribute; validation at source (HR data quality).

### Policy design
Keep policies readable: a few well-defined attributes rather than dozens; document semantics.
questions.code:
~~~rego

default allow := false

# Release allowed for releasers within limit, same region, not under investigation, from a compliant device

    input.action == "release"
    "payments.release" in input.subject.permissions
    input.resource.amount <= input.subject.approval_limit          # fetched from entitlement system, not token
    input.resource.region in input.subject.regions
    not input.subject.under_investigation                           # authoritative HR/security flag, fetched fresh
    input.environment.device_compliant
}

# Missing attributes fall through to default deny
~~~

High-impact attributes fetched fresh from authoritative sources.
Resource attributes set by systems.
Missing attributes mean deny.
Few well-defined attributes; owners and coverage dashboards.

questions.q: The bank uses Azure, AWS and GCP. How do you design workforce and workload identity across clouds without creating separate silos of users and keys?
questions.a:
### Workforce
- One **primary IdP** (Entra ID or Okta) as the source of truth.
- **AWS IAM Identity Center** federated to the IdP (SAML or OIDC) with SCIM provisioning; permission sets mapped from IdP groups; no IAM users for humans.
- **GCP Workforce Identity Federation** or Cloud Identity synced from the IdP; groups mapped to IAM roles.
- Same MFA and conditional access policies applied centrally; just-in-time elevation (PIM groups mapped to permission sets).

### Workloads
- Native identities within each cloud (managed identities, IAM roles, GCP service accounts).
- **Cross-cloud calls via federation**, not keys: AWS workloads assume roles with OIDC from Entra or GitHub; Azure workloads federate to GCP via workload identity pools; GCP to AWS via web identity federation.
- Kubernetes service accounts federated per cloud (EKS IRSA or Pod Identity, AKS workload identity, GKE workload identity).
- SPIFFE/SPIRE for a uniform workload identity layer if multi-cloud service-to-service is heavy.

### Governance
Central inventory of identities and permissions across clouds (CIEM tools), consistent tagging, access reviews spanning clouds, and no long-lived access keys (policy: deny creation).
pts: One primary IdP for workforce across clouds.
AWS Identity Center and GCP workforce federation with SCIM.
Workloads use native identities; cross-cloud via federation.
No long-lived access keys.
CIEM inventory and cross-cloud access reviews.
questions.ex: An audit found 600 AWS IAM users with access keys for engineers who also had Entra accounts; leavers kept AWS keys. Federating AWS through Identity Center from Entra with SCIM, and an SCP blocking IAM user creation, eliminated human IAM users in a quarter.

questions.q: How do you manage human and workload access to Kubernetes clusters securely (authentication, RBAC, kubectl, CI/CD)?
questions.a:
### Human access
- Authenticate with the corporate IdP (AKS with Entra ID, EKS with IAM Identity Center, OIDC for others); **disable local accounts** and static admin credentials.
- RBAC bound to **IdP groups**: namespace-scoped roles for teams (view, edit), cluster roles only for platform engineers via JIT elevation.
- Production: read-only by default; write access through GitOps; kubectl exec into production pods requires elevation and is audited.
- Short-lived credentials (kubelogin tokens), no long-lived kubeconfigs with embedded certificates.

### Workloads
- One **service account per workload**, {{automountServiceAccountToken: false}} unless needed, minimal RBAC (most apps need none).
- Cloud access via workload identity federation, not secrets.

### CI/CD
GitOps (Argo CD) holds cluster access, not CI; Argo CD's own RBAC mapped to IdP groups; projects restrict which namespaces and resources each team can deploy.

### Audit
Kubernetes audit logs to the SIEM: secrets access, exec, RBAC changes, privileged pod creation.

One service account per workload, minimal RBAC.
